content.text: {"title":"Class 5 Maths Revision: Fractions (Chapter 13)","intro":"Let's quickly go over equivalent fractions and comparing fractions using bar models. Read this together with your child before the exam.","sections":[{"heading":"Equivalent Fractions with Bar Models","points":["A fraction shows equal parts of ONE whole, like 1/2 or 3/4.","Equivalent fractions look different but shade the same amount of the bar.","To make an equivalent fraction, always change BOTH the numerator and denominator, not just one.","Always draw both bars the SAME length before comparing shaded parts.","First count how many total parts the bar is cut into, then count shaded parts."],"example":"1/2 is equivalent to 2/4. If you cut a bar into 2 equal parts and shade 1, that is the same amount as cutting it into 4 equal parts and shading 2. The bar length must stay the same both times."},{"heading":"Comparing and Ordering Fractions","points":["Unlike fractions have different denominators, like 1/3 and 1/4.","A bigger denominator means each part is SMALLER, not the fraction itself.","Never decide just by looking at the denominator alone; the numerator matters too.","Use bar models with the same numerator to see how parts shrink as denominator grows.","Ascending order means smallest to biggest; descending means biggest to smallest."],"example":"Compare 1/2 and 1/8. Draw two same-length bars. The bar cut into 2 parts has bigger pieces than the bar cut into 8 parts. So 1/2 is greater than 1/8, even though 8 is a bigger number."}],"remember":["Fraction = numerator (top) over denominator (bottom).","To find an equivalent fraction, multiply or divide top AND bottom by the same number.","Always draw bars the same length before comparing.","More parts (bigger denominator) means smaller pieces, not a bigger fraction.","Check the numerator too, not just the denominator, when comparing fractions."]}
